summary: Most Arabic words are built from a root of three consonants that carries a field of meaning — ط ب خ cooking, ش ر ب drinking, أ ك ل eating, ك ت ب writing — poured into a pattern of vowels and extra letters that gives the kind of word. Patterns are named with the model root ف ع ل (f-ʿ-l): faʿala / yafʿalu is a simple verb (طَبَخَ / يَطْبُخُ), fāʿil the one who does it (طَالِب “student”, from “to seek”), mafʿal a place (مَطْبَخ “kitchen”, مَخْبَز “bakery”, مَكْتَب “office”), mifʿāl a tool (مِفْتَاح “key”, from “to open”). Find the root by removing the article, the prefixes and endings and the long vowels of the pattern; with a root you can guess and remember whole families of words. Weak letters (و، ي) and hamza are root letters too, but they change shape; loanwords (شَاي، بِيرَة، سَلَطَة) stand outside the system.

blocks.title: How to find the root.
blocks.text: Remove the article الْ, the person prefixes of verbs (أَ تَ يَ نَ), the pattern letters مَـ / مُـ, the endings (ة، ـونَ، ـِينَ، ـَاتٌ) and the long vowels ا و ي that the pattern adds. What is left — usually three consonants — is the root.

blocks.title: Weak letters hide.
blocks.text: و and ي can be root letters that turn into long vowels or vanish: أَرَادَ / يُرِيدُ has the root ر و د; اِشْتَرَى / يَشْتَرِي has ش ر ي — the ت is the form VIII pattern, not the root. A doubled root hides under the šadda: أَحَبَّ = ح ب ب.

blocks.title: Hamza is a consonant.
blocks.text: أَكَلَ has the root ء ك ل: the hamza is the first root letter. In آكُلُ (“I eat”) it melts with the prefix into آ.
Not every word has a root you can use: loanwords like شَاي, بِيرَة, سَلَطَة and أَرُزّ stand outside the system.
Hebrew works the same way — often with the same roots: Arabic ك ت ب / Hebrew כ־ת־ב (to write), Arabic ل ح م “meat” / Hebrew לֶחֶם “bread”, Arabic ط ب خ “cook” / Hebrew ט־ב־ח “slaughter”.

askYourself: Which letters are left when I remove al-, the prefixes, the endings and the pattern letters (مَـ، مُـ، the long vowels)?
Are ا و ي part of the pattern or of the root? (كَاتِب: the ا is the pattern; يُرِيدُ: the ي stands for the root letter و.)
Is there a šadda? It may hide a doubled root letter (أَحَبَّ = ح ب ب) or belong to the pattern (مُعَلِّم, form II; طَبَّاخ, faʿʿāl).
Does the word start with a hamza? It can be a root letter (أَكَلَ) or a pattern letter (أَرَادَ, form IV).
Do I know another word with the same three letters? Then the meanings are related.
Is it a loanword (شَاي، بِيرَة، سَلَطَة)? Then there is no root to look for.

traps: The ت of اِشْتَرَى is the pattern of form VIII, not a root letter: the root is ش ر ي.
The م of مَطْبَخ, مَكْتَب and مِفْتَاح belongs to the pattern (place, tool), not to the root.
The long vowels of a pattern are not root letters: طَالِب = ط ل ب, not *ط ا ل ب.
The same letters in another order are another root: مِلْح (م ل ح, salt) and لَحْم (ل ح م, meat) are not related.
Not everything with three consonants is a root word: شَاي and بِيرَة are borrowings.

quiz.q: What is the root of مَطْبَخ (kitchen)?
quiz.why: مَـ … is the place pattern mafʿal; the root is ط ب خ, as in طَبَخَ (to cook).

quiz.q: Which word shares a root with شَرِبَ (to drink)?
quiz.why: ش ر ب in both. شَاي is a loanword with no Arabic root.

quiz.q: What does the pattern مَفْعَل usually make?
quiz.why: مَطْبَخ kitchen, مَخْبَز bakery, مَكْتَب office. Tools are mifʿāl (مِفْتَاح), persons fāʿil (كَاتِب).

quiz.q: What is the root of يُرِيدُ (he wants)?
quiz.why: يُـ is the prefix; the ī stands for the weak root letter و (form IV أَرَادَ, verbal noun إِرَادَة).

quiz.q: What is the root of اِشْتَرَى (to buy)?
quiz.why: The ت is the infix of form VIII (iftaʿala); the final ā stands for the root letter ي.

quiz.q: Which word shares a root with مِلْح (salt)?
quiz.why: م ل ح in both; مَالِح is the fāʿil pattern. لَحْم has ل ح م — the same letters in another order make another root.

quiz.q: Which word shares a root with كِتَاب (book)?
quiz.why: مَـ + ك ت ب: the place where you write.
مُـ … ـِّـ is the participle of form II (mufaʿʿil); عِلْم = knowledge: a teacher “makes know”.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew builds words the same way (שֹׁרֶשׁ + מִשְׁקָל / בִּנְיָן) and shares many roots with Arabic: כ־ת־ב / ك ت ب “write”, ל־ח־ם / ل ح م (bread / meat).
German has a faint echo in its strong verbs: the vowel inside the root changes (trinken – trank – getrunken), as Arabic patterns change the vowels around ش ر ب.
Chinese words never change inside; new words are made by putting characters side by side (茶 tea + 杯 cup = 茶杯) instead of patterns.

notes.text: Greek builds words from stems and endings (γράφω, γραφείο, γράμμα); Arabic weaves three root consonants into vowel patterns (كَتَبَ, مَكْتَب, كِتَاب). أَرُزّ (rice) is the same word as ὄρυζα, borrowed through Aramaic — a loan with no usable root.
Russian builds families with prefixes and suffixes on a stem (писать, писатель, письмо); Arabic changes the vowels and adds letters around a root of consonants (كَتَبَ, كَاتِب, كِتَاب).
English keeps traces of the idea in sing / sang / song; in Arabic it is the main way to make words: ك ت ب → كَتَبَ, كَاتِب, كِتَاب, مَكْتَب.
Spanish builds words with suffixes (cocinar, cocina, cocinero); Arabic with patterns around a root: طَبَخَ (cook), مَطْبَخ (kitchen), طَبَّاخ (a cook).
French cuisine, cuisinier add suffixes to a stem; Arabic puts the root ط ب خ into patterns: مَطْبَخ (kitchen), طَبَّاخ (cook).
Hindi borrowed whole Arabic word families through Persian — इल्म (knowledge), आलिम (scholar), मालूम (known) all come from ع ل م; in Arabic the patterns behind them are living rules.
Persian is full of Arabic words, so many patterns look familiar: کتاب, کاتب, مکتب (ک ت ب); علم, عالم, معلم (ع ل م). شَاي came into Arabic from Persian چای — a loan with no Arabic root.
Marathi builds words with prefixes and suffixes on a stem; Arabic weaves a consonant root into patterns: ك ت ب → كِتَاب, كَاتِب, مَكْتَب.

Turkish already has whole Arabic root families: kitap, kâtip (clerk), mektup (letter), mektep (school) all come from ك ت ب; ilim, âlim, muallim, malumat from ع ل م. In Arabic you learn the patterns behind them.
Japanese makes new words by combining kanji and adding endings; Arabic changes the vowels inside a consonant root.
Finnish adds suffixes to an unchanging stem (kirja, kirjasto, kirjailija); Arabic keeps three consonants and changes everything around them (كِتَاب, مَكْتَبَة, كَاتِب).
Hungarian adds suffixes to an unchanging stem; Arabic changes the vowels inside the root.
Swahili borrowed Arabic word families too: kitabu (book), katibu (secretary), maktaba (library) — all ك ت ب. In Arabic the pattern is a living rule.
Luganda builds words with class prefixes and verb extensions; Arabic changes the vowel pattern around a consonant root.
Vietnamese words never change inside; new words are made by combining syllables. Arabic makes them by pouring a root into patterns.
Inuktitut builds long words by adding suffix after suffix to a stem; Arabic keeps words short and changes the vowels and added letters around a root of three consonants.
